system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2197-05-30 12:51:00 to 2197-06-01 14:57:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, multiple prior stents, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, type 2 diabetes, and antiphospholipid syndrome presented with chest pain during a scheduled endoscopy, found to have an aborted inferior STEMI. Initial evaluation showed subtherapeutic INR of 1.4 and normal initial troponin, which later peaked at 0.16. Coronary angiography revealed stable coronary anatomy with no new intervenable lesions. He was managed with heparin infusion and transitioned to warfarin 6 mg daily, with continuation of dual antiplatelet therapy. His metoprolol was reduced to 150 mg and valsartan to 80 mg due to orthostasis, and diltiazem was discontinued. Insulin was adjusted for glucose control. He remained stable, with INR reaching 2.5 at discharge. He was discharged home on optimized medical therapy with follow-up planned in primary care, cardiology, and anticoagulation clinics.
problems: Atherosclerotic heart disease of native coronary artery with unspecified angina pectoris
Hypertensive heart disease with heart failure
Presence of coronary angioplasty implant and graft
Type 2 diabetes mellitus with unspecified diabetic retinopathy without macular edema
Personal history of other venous thrombosis and embolism

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with chest pain today. Can you tell me more about what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was late for my clinic appointment, so I started walking fast. That’s when the chest pain started—right in the middle, crushing. I had to sit down for about 15 minutes before it got better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Did you have your nitroglycerin with you?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I forgot it. But when I got to the clinic, they sent me to the ER, and they gave me nitro there. It helped a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had this kind of pain before when walking?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, almost every time. But today was worse. I also have this pressure in my stomach that didn’t go away with the nitro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you. We’ve checked your EKG and your troponin levels—both came back normal, no signs of a heart attack. But given your history, we want to be cautious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many stents. I was worried this was something new.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know your history well. Because of your coronary disease, we started you on IV nitroglycerin and heparin to prevent any clotting while we figure things out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I have this IV? I feel fine now—no chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the IV is for the medications. We’ll keep it going for now. We also did a chest X-ray, and it showed no pneumonia or other issues—your lungs look clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. But what about the stomach pressure? That’s been bothering me for weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. It doesn’t seem related to your heart. You mentioned it sometimes gets better with eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I’ve been taking Maalox and calcium carbonate. They help a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. You had an endoscopy recently, and it was normal, so that’s reassuring. We’ll continue managing it as an outpatient issue with your GI doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a CT scan of the abdomen scheduled soon. Should I still go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll make sure you’re prepped properly, especially since you might need premedication for contrast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And my heart—do you think this was just my usual angina?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely. We’re going to do an exercise stress test tomorrow to confirm. If it doesn’t reproduce your symptoms or show changes on the EKG, that supports stable angina.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope I can do it. My legs get tired fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay—we’ll stop if you need to. The goal is safety. We’ll also keep monitoring your blood work. Your white count is a bit low, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You completed the stress test this morning. You stopped due to leg fatigue, but importantly, no chest pain and no EKG changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel any chest pain. Just couldn’t keep going on the treadmill.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s actually very reassuring. It means your heart didn’t show signs of ischemia at that level of exertion. So we’re confident this was stable angina, not an unstable event.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m not having a heart attack?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. Your heart muscle is fine—no damage. But because your angina seems to be worsening, we’re starting you on a new medication called Imdur, which is a long-acting nitrate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried that before. Gave me bad headaches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ll start low and monitor. It can help reduce how often you get chest pain when walking. We also stopped the IV heparin since you’re back on your Xarelto.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my aspirin? I’ve been on that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. You’re on three blood thinners—Plavix, Xarelto, and aspirin. That’s called triple therapy, and it increases bleeding risk. Since you had a possible past stomach bleed, we stopped the aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But won’t that increase my risk for clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not significantly. For your condition, Plavix and Xarelto are enough. Your cardiologist will discuss whether aspirin is needed long-term at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my diabetes meds? I noticed my insulin was adjusted.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we lowered your long-acting insulin while you were not eating much. But we’ll restart your full dose at home, along with metformin, which we held in the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—everything else stays the same?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, including your blood pressure, cholesterol, and pain medications. We’ll send a full list with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. Your condition is stable, and we’ve addressed the main concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. So what’s the plan after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your medications as listed, especially the new Imdur. Watch for headaches and let your doctor know. Keep your GI follow-up and CT scan. And call your cardiologist to discuss the aspirin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I get chest pain again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use your nitroglycerin as before—one every five minutes, up to three. If it doesn’t help, or if you feel worse, go to the ER immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing it wasn’t a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—my daughter is picking me up. Can she come in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’ll have the nurse go over discharge instructions with both of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay safe, and keep managing those symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon, I hope not as a patient!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hopefully not! Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease, multiple stents, antiphospholipid syndrome, type 2 diabetes, and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction presented with exertional substernal chest pain that was worse than usual. He had no EKG changes or elevated troponins, but due to his high-risk history, he was admitted for observation and treated with IV nitroglycerin and heparin. His chest pain resolved and did not recur. An exercise stress test showed no ischemic changes, supporting stable angina. He was started on isosorbide mononitrate (Imdur) for angina prophylaxis. Aspirin was discontinued due to triple antithrombotic therapy and a history concerning for prior gastrointestinal bleeding. His abdominal pain, which was unrelated to cardiac issues, will continue to be evaluated as an outpatient with a scheduled CT scan. He remained stable, was discharged home on optimized medical therapy, and advised to follow up with cardiology and primary care.
